title: David with the Head of Goliath

image.credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (David with the Head of Goliath-Caravaggio (1610).jpg)

phase.label: Exile and the last years, c. 1605–1610 (dating disputed)

source.label: David with the Head of Goliath

highlight.text: Chiaroscuro was practised long before he came on the scene, but it was Caravaggio who made the technique a dominant stylistic element, darkening the shadows and transfixing the subject in a blinding shaft of light.

work.text: Caravaggio captures the drama more effectively by having the head dangling from David's hand and dripped out blood, rather than resting on a ledge.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)

work.text: The decision to depict him as pensive and resigned rather than jubilant creates an unusual psychological bond between him and Goliath.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)

moment.text: The sword in David's hand carries an abbreviated inscription H-AS OS; this has been interpreted as an abbreviation of the Latin phrase humilitas occidit superbiam ("humility kills pride").

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)

moment.text: David and Goliath standing for Christ and Satan and the triumph of good over evil in orthodox Christian iconography of the period

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)

matters.text: This bond is further complicated by the fact that Caravaggio has depicted himself as Goliath, while the model for David is il suo Caravaggino ("his own little Caravaggio").

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)

matters.text: If the painting was a gift to Cardinal Borghese, the papal official with the power to grant Caravaggio a pardon for murder, it can also be interpreted as a personal plea for mercy.
